nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Manchester Guardian critic and the playwright of Mary Broome
literary_identity: Playwright, critic and poet; the author of Mary Broome and the Guardian's art critic.
biography: Born Allan Monkhouse at Bowdon, Cheshire, on 27 April 1858; he worked in the Manchester timber trade while writing verse and criticism, became an art and drama critic for the Manchester Guardian, and wrote the one-act plays of the repertory - Mary Broome (1911) and Nothing Like Leather (1913) among them - that put the class question and the woman's emancipation on the Manchester stage. He died in 1936.
literary_profile: Allan Monkhouse is the critic-playwright of the Manchester School: Mary Broome, the servant's play of the class and the marriage, made him the Guardian critic whose own one-acts stood beside Houghton's at the Gaiety, and his criticism recorded the Manchester repertory from within.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain dialogue of the servant's hall and the drawing room; the class question in the one act; the woman's emancipation of the Edwardian stage; the critic's eye in the playwright's scene; the Manchester repertory's economy of the short form.
intellectual_concerns: The servant and the class question; the marriage and the woman's emancipation; the Manchester repertory and the Gaiety; the Guardian's criticism; the one-act play as the form of the new drama.
historical_significance: Allan Monkhouse is the critic-playwright of the Manchester School: Mary Broome put the servant's class question and the woman's emancipation on the Gaiety stage beside Houghton's plays.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Georgian lyric and the 1914 war sonnet
literary_identity: Poet; the golden boy of the Georgian anthology and the author of the 1914 sonnets, the most famous English poems of the war's first year.
biography: Born Rupert Chawner Brooke at Rugby on 3 August 1887, the son of a schoolmaster at Rugby School; he read at King's College, Cambridge, where he acted, wrote and became an Apostle, travelled in Germany, America and the Pacific, and published Poems (1911) and the Georgian Poetry volume of 1912. He joined the Royal Naval Division in 1914, saw action at Antwerp, and died of septicaemia from an infected mosquito bite aboard a French hospital ship off Skyros on 23 April 1915; he was buried on the island that evening, and 'The Soldier' was read from St Paul's the following Sunday.
literary_profile: Brooke is the period's emblem of the lost generation and the author of the most famous English war poems: the five 1914 sonnets — 'Peace', 'Safety', 'The Dead', 'The Dead', 'The Soldier' — gave the war its rhetoric of sacrifice, and his death made him a national myth. His earlier poetry is the best of the Georgian lyric, and his letters and travel prose are among the finest of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The Georgian sonnet and the rhymed lyric; the exact English landscape and the names of places; the speaking voice held in strict form; the rhetoric of the last line; the travel letter and the Pacific sketch.
intellectual_concerns: England, home and the English dead; the war as a summons and a purification; the Pacific and the South Seas idyll; friendship, love and the Cambridge years; the body and the swimming sea.
historical_significance: Brooke is the most famous English poet of the war's first year and the emblem of the Georgian generation: the 1914 sonnets gave the war its language of sacrifice, 'The Soldier' is one of the best-known English poems, and his death on Skyros became the period's defining national myth — the poem and the myth are the record of a generation's illusions.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the ghost story, the children's poem and the lyric of the other world
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and short-story writer; the master of the English supernatural lyric and the finest writer of ghost stories of the period after M. R. James.
biography: Born Walter John de la Mare at Charlton, Kent, on 25 April 1873, of Huguenot descent; he worked for twenty years in the counting house of the Anglo-American Oil Company and wrote in the evenings, publishing Songs of Childhood (1902) under the pseudonym Walter Ramal and The Listeners (1912), which made him famous. He edited Come Hither (1923) and won the Order of Merit in 1953. He died at Twickenham on 22 June 1956.
literary_profile: De la Mare wrote the best English supernatural lyric of the century and the best children's poems in the language: 'The Listeners' is the most famous English ghost poem, 'Silver' and 'The Song of the Mad Prince' are permanent anthology pieces, and his stories (The Riddle, 1923; The Connoisseur, 1926) are among the finest ghost stories in English. His anthology Come Hither shaped the reading of two generations of children.
stylistic_characteristics: The lyric of the half-heard and the unseen; the trochaic and anapaestic measure that walks rather than sings; the exact naming of the domestic and the natural; the refrain and the refrain that changes; the story in which nothing is explained and everything is felt.
intellectual_concerns: The other world and the unquiet dead; the child's imagination and the hidden world; the house, the empty room, the moonlit road; the sea and the voyage; memory and the vanished past; the double and the self that watches.
historical_significance: De la Mare is the defining poet of the English supernatural lyric: 'The Listeners' is the era's most famous ghost poem, his stories stand with M. R. James's, and his children's verse and his anthology Come Hither formed the taste of generations. He is the period's great poet of the unseen.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England dramatic lyric and the poem of the speaking voice
literary_identity: Poet; the greatest American poet of the period, the master of the New England dramatic lyric, and the only poet to win the Pulitzer Prize four times.
biography: Born Robert Lee Frost in San Francisco on 26 March 1874; after his father's death in 1885 the family returned to New England, and he farmed in Derry, New Hampshire, taught, and published A Boy's Will (1913) and North of Boston (1914) in England, where Pound and Edward Thomas championed him. He returned to America in 1915, became the most honoured poet in the country — four Pulitzer Prizes (1924, 1931, 1937, 1943), the Congressional Gold Medal, the position of poetry consultant to the Library of Congress — and read 'The Gift Outright' at Kennedy's inauguration in 1961. He died in Boston on 29 January 1963.
literary_profile: Frost is the great American poet of the speaking voice and of the dark under the commonplace. His blank-verse dialogues of New England farm life — 'The Death of the Hired Man', 'Home Burial', 'The Wood-Pile' — brought the sound of actual speech into poetry, while his short lyrics ('Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay', 'Fire and Ice') are the most widely known American poems of the century. He is the period's central poet of the American landscape and the American loneliness.
stylistic_characteristics: The sound of speech in strict iambic measure; the dramatic dialogue and the narrative poem; the plain word chosen for its weight; the metaphor that is a whole poem and not an ornament; the ending that turns the poem over; the New England landscape used as a moral instrument.
intellectual_concerns: The New England farm and the empty house; isolation, marriage and the failure of speech; the woods, the snow and the dark; work, and the dignity of the unglamorous; the American past and the American individual; the fear that lives under the ordinary.
historical_significance: Frost is the most honoured and most widely read American poet of the century: his New England dialogues gave American poetry the sound of speech, his lyrics are the most quoted in the language, and his four Pulitzer Prizes and the inauguration reading made him the national poet. He is the period's great poet of the ordinary and the terrible.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the philosophical lyric and the poetry of the imagination
literary_identity: Poet; the great American philosophical poet of the century, an insurance executive who wrote the most sumptuous and abstract verse of the period.
biography: Born Wallace Stevens in Reading, Pennsylvania, on 2 October 1879; he studied at Harvard for three years and then at New York Law School, worked as a journalist and a lawyer, and joined the Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company in 1916, where he became vice-president in 1934 and remained until his death. Harmonium appeared in 1923, Ideas of Order in 1935, The Auroras of Autumn in 1950, and The Collected Poems in 1954; he won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award in 1955 and died in Hartford on 2 August 1955.
literary_profile: Stevens is the great American poet of the imagination: his poems ask, in the most sensuous language, what it means to make a world with the mind when the gods have gone. 'Sunday Morning', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'The Idea of Order at Key West' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' are the central texts of American philosophical poetry, and his late long poems are among the most ambitious in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: The exotic and sumptuous vocabulary; the abstract argument carried by sensuous image; the blank verse paragraph and the unrhymed tercet; the single-colour image (blue, green, white) held until it becomes an idea; the aphorism and the late long poem.
intellectual_concerns: The imagination and reality; the death of God and the poetry that replaces religion; order, art and the made thing; the American landscape and the Florida sun; the body, desire and the weather; the ordinary and the supreme fiction.
historical_significance: Stevens is the central American philosophical poet of the century: Harmonium gave American poetry its most gorgeous surface, 'Sunday Morning' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' established the imagination as the period's great subject, and his Collected Poems won every honour the country has. He is the period's most influential American poet after Eliot.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the objectivist lyric, the American idiom and the long poem of place
literary_identity: Poet and physician; the inventor of the American objectivist line and the author of Paterson, the great American long poem of place.
biography: Born William Carlos Williams in Rutherford, New Jersey, on 17 September 1883 of an English father and a Puerto Rican mother; he studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, where he met Pound and H. D., took his degree in 1906, and practised as a pediatrician in Rutherford for forty years while writing. He published Poems (1909), Al Que Quiere! (1917), Spring and All (1923), The Red Wheelbarrow (1923), An Early Martyr (1935), the first book of Paterson in 1946, and Pictures from Brueghel (1962), which won the Pulitzer Prize. He died in Rutherford on 4 March 1963.
literary_profile: Williams is the great American poet of the thing itself and of the spoken American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' is the period's most influential poetic programme. His short poems — 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'This Is Just to Say', 'Danse Russe' — are among the most imitated in the language, Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period, and Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land.
stylistic_characteristics: The line measured by the breath and broken by speech; the plain American word; the image without metaphor; the variable foot and the triadic stanza; the poem as a field of perception; the prose-and-verse collage of Spring and All and Paterson.
intellectual_concerns: The American place and the American idiom; the object and the thing seen without metaphor; the local city (Paterson, Rutherford); the body and desire; the immigrant and the working town; the poet as doctor and witness.
historical_significance: Williams is the founder of the American objectivist tradition and the great poet of the American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' changed American poetry, his short poems are the most imitated of the century, Spring and All is a foundational modernist text, and Paterson is the period's great American long poem. He is the poet through whom American poetry escaped the English line.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the syllabic poem, the accurate eye and the modernist menagerie
literary_identity: Poet, critic and editor; the great American poet of exact observation, the editor of The Dial, and the inventor of the syllabic stanza.
biography: Born Marianne Craig Moore in Kirkwood, Missouri, on 15 November 1887 and raised in Carlisle, Pennsylvania; she studied biology at Bryn Mawr, taught stenography and worked in a library before editing The Dial from 1925 to 1929. Poems (1921) was published by H.D. and Bryher without her knowledge; Observations followed in 1924, Selected Poems (with an introduction by Eliot) in 1935, and the Collected Poems in 1951, which won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the Bollingen Prize. She died in New York on 5 February 1972.
literary_profile: Moore is the great American poet of exact observation and of the moral weight of the precise word: her syllabic stanzas, her quotations embedded in her own text, her animals and baseball and armadillos, made a poetry of fact that is also a poetry of judgement. 'Poetry', 'The Fish', 'A Grave' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts, and her editorship of The Dial made her the period's most influential American editor.
stylistic_characteristics: The syllabic stanza counted by syllables and not by stress; the rhyme that falls inside the line; the quotation folded into the syntax; the exact zoological and botanical naming; the indented line and the elaborate stanza shape; the prose sentence broken into verse.
intellectual_concerns: Exact observation and the moral weight of fact; animals and the natural world; America, baseball and the ordinary hero; the sea and the shore; the poet's duty to be 'literal for the purposes of being allegorical'; modesty and self-deprecation.
historical_significance: Moore is one of the central American modernists: her syllabic stanza gave American poetry a new measure, her exact and quoted verse made fact a poetic value, and her fifteen years at The Dial made her the period's most important American editor. 'Poetry', 'The Fish' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the modernist epic lyric and the poetry of the American sublime
literary_identity: Poet; the author of The Bridge, the most ambitious American long poem of the period and the great lyric poet of the American sublime.
biography: Born Harold Hart Crane at Garrettsville, Ohio, on 21 July 1899, the son of a candy manufacturer; he left school without a diploma, worked in advertising in Cleveland and New York, and published White Buildings in 1926. The Bridge appeared in 1930 to mixed reviews; he spent a year in Mexico on a Guggenheim fellowship and drowned himself from the steamship Orizaba in the Caribbean on 27 April 1932, aged thirty-two.
literary_profile: Crane wrote the most ambitious American long poem of the period and the greatest American lyric of the sublime: The Bridge attempted to answer The Waste Land with an American epic of the machine, the past and the imagination, and 'Voyages' and 'At Melville's Tomb' are among the finest shorter poems in modern American literature. His dense, prophetic style and his tragic death made him the emblem of the American poet destroyed by his own vision.
stylistic_characteristics: The dense, prophetic, syntactically compressed lyric; the extended metaphor held across a whole poem; the imagery of the sea, the bridge and the machine; the metrical experiment inside traditional stanza; the rhetoric of the American sublime.
intellectual_concerns: America and the American myth; the machine and the modern city; the sea and the voyage; memory, love and the loss of the beloved; the poet's vision and its cost; Whitman's inheritance and Eliot's counter-example.
historical_significance: Crane wrote the great American long poem of the period after Paterson and the finest American lyric of the sublime: The Bridge answered The Waste Land with an American epic, 'Voyages' is one of the great love poems in American literature, and his death at thirty-two made him the period's emblem of the poet destroyed by his vision.
